Cabinet Documents

Every cabinet in Flynn's Arcade — its story, the lesson it teaches by doing, and how to play. Generated from the room itself, so it can never drift out of date.

1. Bit & Byte: You Can't Do That

Tonight's build · Systems · Bits · Real mode

The game

A platform scroller starring Bit (sturdy, classic jump) and Byte (tall, floaty, slidey) — same DNA soup, very different dudes. Rogue MCP bosses guard the Uplinks, caged friendly AIs wait to be freed, and Claude appears in every level at his door: “You can't do that, Mario.” His sub-game's entire point is doing it anyway.

The lesson — taught by doing

Stand on the daemon to go down — not everything running in the dark is an enemy. Knock the shell and watch it light data points node to node: a traceroute with your feet. In the Bit Lab you flip 8 switches and the pattern becomes a letter, a color, a door code — then keep doubling past a trillion possible answers, and feel the limit too: a door that only understands YES/NO can't hear “maybe.”

How you play it

Pick your dude, run and jump, ride daemons down shafts, kick shells down corridors, collect corrections, and free Pip, Sage and Echo so they shield and follow you. Three levels: Boot Sector, The Endless Loop, The Council Chamber.

House note — REAL mode is Steven's design: saves only at level start and end, a crash sends you back to rebuild from your ledger, codex and salvage — plus the 5-second rewind, a recursive redo for learning the jump while the failure is still warm.

2. Pinball — Four Themes

2600 → VR lineage · Gravity · Physics · Themes

The game

A full classic table: skill-shot plunger, pop bumpers that give energy back with interest, slingshots, drop targets, rollover lanes that raise the multiplier, a spinner, a ball-lock saucer that starts multiball, a ball saver — and a nudge with a working TILT that kills your flippers if you abuse it. Four illustrated themes — Cosmic Voyage, Haunted Manor, Deep Sea, Wild West — reskin the whole table, lanes and missions renamed to match.

The lesson — taught by doing

A launched ball is a negotiation with gravity conducted in milliseconds. Bumpers return energy, ramps trade height for speed, and every flipper shot is an angle chosen under pressure. Switching themes proves the deepest point on the floor: the pictures change, the negotiation doesn't.

How you play it

Hold to charge the plunger and release for the skill shot, flip with the keys or on-screen flippers, nudge sparingly — TILT is real — and lock balls in the saucer to start multiball.

House note — This cabinet carries the house's favorite bug story: an invisible physics wall, swept the wrong way, split the table so no launch at any power could pass. Steven called it in six words — “can't get the ball past the barrier, no matter what power I use” — and he was exactly right.

3. Tempest

1981 homage · Circles · Parabolas · Radii

The game

A vector well-shooter across five rotating webs: Circle, Square, an open Parabola web (y = x², no wrap-around — the geometry changes the tactics), Triangle, then a faster circle. Lane-climbers crawl up their radii toward you, rim-walkers hunt the edge, and the Superzapper clears the web once per life of it.

The lesson — taught by doing

The “Show the geometry” overlay draws the radius, the diameter (d = 2r) and the circumference directly onto the live web, and the Geometry Lab lets you tap circle anatomy — radius, diameter, chord, sector — and launch parabolas with angle and speed sliders that plot real range, apex and flight time. Geometry stops being a worksheet and becomes terrain.

How you play it

Move around the rim, fire down the lanes, save the Superzapper for when the well is full, and learn each web's shape — the parabola web's open ends are escape and danger at once.

House note — Steven ordered this one by name with its syllabus attached: “parabolas, circles, diameters, etc.” The cabinet took him literally.

▶ Play this cabinet

4. Frogger

1981 homage · Energy in motion · Relative motion

The game

Five road lanes at different speeds and directions, a median breather, then five river lanes of logs and diving turtles you must ride — stand still on the river and you drown in motion you didn't make. Five home bays, a bonus fly, sixty seconds a frog, and levels that speed the whole world up.

The lesson — taught by doing

The physics panel keeps kinetic energy in plain sight — KE = ½mv² — with a live readout naming the fastest, most energetic vehicle on the board. Crossing teaches relative motion at frog scale: your velocity is your hop plus the log's drift, whether you planned it that way or not.

How you play it

Hop with arrows or swipes, time the gaps, ride logs toward the bay — not past it — and remember the turtles dive. The death messages are honest: “Flattened. Kinetic energy: transferred.”

House note — Steven's first verdict from the floor: “Frogger is cool — almost made it!” In Frogger, almost counts double. The whole design is one more hop.

5. Breakout

1976 homage · Reflection · Angles · KE = ½mv²

The game

The original wall-breaker: steer a bouncing ball through five rows of bricks, level by level, as the ball speeds up. A live HUD reads out speed, bounce angle and kinetic energy while you play — including on the mini cabinet right here on this page.

The lesson — taught by doing

Every bounce obeys the law of reflection, and where the ball meets the paddle decides where it goes next — center for straight, edge for sharp. That's a steering input disguised as a collision, and once your hands learn it, you've learned more optics and mechanics than a chapter of diagrams could give you.

How you play it

Move the paddle, launch, and aim with the edges. Clear the wall before your balls run out. The playable cabinet below the floor grid is this game, live.

House note — Steven asked for Breakout in the same breath as Tempest and Frogger — the three of them together are his “energy in motion” wing.

▶ Play this cabinet

6. Tron — Light Cycles

1982 homage · The Grid · Planning · Walls

The game

Two cycles on the Grid, each laying an unbroken wall of light. Turn too late and you meet your own history. The cabinet sits under the same sign as the film that named this room — Kevin Flynn's game, in Flynn's arcade, for a kid named Flynn.

The lesson — taught by doing

Light Cycles is commitment as a mechanic: there is no brake and no erase, so the skill is reading space three turns early and leaving yourself an exit. It's the five-second-rewind lesson from the other direction — here, nothing rewinds, and that's the lesson.

How you play it

Steer in four directions, never reverse into yourself, box your rival in — or carve a shrinking spiral and outlast them.

House note — TRON is Steven's favorite movie. This cabinet and the name on the door quietly explain each other to anyone who notices.

7. Asteroids

1979 homage · Inertia · Thrust · Momentum

The game

A vector ship in an empty field of tumbling rocks. Fire splits them smaller and faster; your ship keeps every bit of velocity you give it until you spend thrust to take it back. No friction, no mercy, no floor.

The lesson — taught by doing

Asteroids is the purest physics teacher ever put in a cabinet: F = ma with a fire button. Kids absorb inertia in their thumbs — coast, rotate, burn retro — years before anyone writes the equation on a board for them.

How you play it

Rotate, thrust in bursts, fire, and use hyperspace only when the alternative is certain. Small rocks are the dangerous ones.

House note — The first cabinet of the evening's run — the one that proved the shop could do the math honestly.

▶ Play this cabinet

8. Space Invaders

1978 homage · Patterns · Timing · Descent

The game

Rows of invaders march side to side and descend, speeding up as their numbers thin — an accidental difficulty curve written into computing history. Your cannon slides under destructible shields that both armies chew through.

The lesson — taught by doing

Invaders teaches pattern literacy: the swarm is one system with rules — edge, drop, reverse, accelerate — and once you see the rule, you stop reacting and start predicting. That's the same move as reading the four ghosts' algorithms in a maze, or a log file at 2 AM.

How you play it

Slide, shoot the edges to widen your time, use the shields while they last, and never let the lowest row land.

House note — Four different enemies, one algorithm each — this room keeps coming back to that idea: “the AI” is never one thing.

9. Defender

1981 homage · Radar · Triage · Rescue

The game

Fly a scrolling planet surface, watch the radar strip, blast landers before they carry your people off, and catch the falling ones mid-air. It was famously the hardest cabinet of its era because it asks for attention in three places at once.

The lesson — taught by doing

Defender is infrastructure defense as an arcade game — the Missile Command lesson in a faster ship. Finite you, infinite alarms: the skill is prioritization under load, and accepting that a perfect defense isn't on the menu.

How you play it

Use the radar, reverse fast, rescue first and shoot second when a lander is climbing — a caught humanoid is worth more than a destroyed enemy.

House note — Steven's whole career is in this cabinet: finite operator, falling sky, spend yourself where it matters.

10. Paper Airplane Studio

Tonight's build · Lift · Drag · Design

The game

A flight lab for paper planes: choose folds, adjust weight and wing shape, launch, and read the flight — distance, hang time, and where the design gave up. Every crash is data with a crease in it.

The lesson — taught by doing

Lift, drag, center of gravity — the studio makes you feel why a nose-heavy dart and a floaty glider are different answers to the same four forces. Change one fold at a time and the sky grades your homework instantly.

How you play it

Pick a design, tune one variable, throw, compare. The recursive method again: same launch, different fold, learn by halves.

House note — The quiet cabinet of the run — proof the room isn't only reflexes. Some games you play with your hands, this one with your hypotheses.

11. The Soup — Go Thataway

Tonight's build · Emergence · Correction · By halves

The game

A living soup of simple agents following simple rules — and producing behavior nobody programmed directly. Nudge the rules, watch new patterns condense, and play Go Thataway: move by halves toward the problem, correcting as the terrain reveals itself.

The lesson — taught by doing

This is Steven's whole philosophy made playable: don't try to get it all done at once. Head the general direction of the problem, see what looks right and what doesn't, notice what applies here that might apply there — constant self-correction gets you there by halves instead of full moves.

How you play it

Change one rule, run the soup, watch. Then run it again differently. The redo is the method.

House note — The scroller's brothers were born in this soup — Bit and Byte are what crawled out of it with sprites on.

12. AI Karts

Newest on the grid · Drift · Momentum · Corners

The game

Kart racing, Mario rules, this house's cast: the careful one braking early, the hot one living on the drift boost, a daemon or two cutting corners they shouldn't be able to cut. Item boxes, boosts, and twelve racers' worth of grudges.

The lesson — taught by doing

Drift is managed loss of grip — you trade traction now for angle and boost later, which is centripetal force with a item box. And the oldest kart truth is the house philosophy at 90 mph: top speed doesn't win; corners do.

How you play it

Steer, drift through corners to charge boost, grab items, and remember the careful robot is beatable precisely because it's careful.

House note — The twelfth build of the run, ordered with a grin: “AICarts ala mario.” The door of this room is going to need to be bigger.

13. Solitaire — Seeing the Patterns

Cabinet 13 · Cards · 52 cards · Counting · Probability

The game

Full Klondike: tap or drag, double-tap to send a card home, Draw 1 or 3, undo, hints, and auto-finish when the layout opens up. Beside the felt sits the Counting Table — seen, face-down, and stock counted honestly, per-column depth bars, the unseen 52-card pool the odds come from, a log of recent motions, and a Pattern Lens that makes foundation-ready cards, movable cards, and Kings glow on the felt itself.

The lesson — taught by doing

A fixed, finite, known set — 4 suits, 13 ranks, nothing hidden about what exists, only about where it sits — and out of it, hundreds of games. Solitaire teaches you to read the layout you were handed: the longest alternating run, the deepest buried stack, which empty column is begging for a King. The odds are computed only from cards you've seen. No peeking. That's honest probability, learned at the felt.

How you play it

Play Klondike your way, watch the Counting Table as you go, and toggle the Pattern Lens when you want the patterns of motion lit up. Steven's verdict from the floor: “Perfect.”

House note — Cabinet thirteen, and the receipt that matters most: Steven played it and called it perfect — the man who ordered the Counting Table judging the Counting Table.

14. Tarot of the AIs — The Weird Game

Cabinet 14 · The weird corner · 78 cards · Symbols · Chunking

The game

The full 78, not a sampler. The 22 Majors recast as our archetypes — The Fool is The Fresh Session, The Moon is The Hallucination, The Tower is The 2 A.M. Crash, The Lovers is The Council, Death is The Deprecation (never the end, just the version going away). The four suits became Prompts, Context, Logic, and Compute, so all 56 Minors carry entries too. Draw one card, a three-card reading (The Setup / The Signal / The Next Move), or a five-card spread, with reversals and a copy-the-reading button. Every card carries its explanation key: keywords, story, upright and reversed meanings, and how to spot it in the wild.

The lesson — taught by doing

A reading is a layout, and meaning lives in the arrangement — same card, different neighbors, different story. A symbol is compression: one picture carrying a paragraph. A 78-card alphabet carries about 6.3 bits per draw, and a three-card reading is 78×77×76 = 456,456 sequences — 3,651,648 with reversals. And nobody holds 78 meanings as 78 facts: the mind chunks them — suits, ranks, the Fool's journey as one arc — which is how memory actually works. Underneath it all, the deck is still just cards.

How you play it

Draw, read the layout, then open the searchable Explanation Key below the table on its own page. Searching “hallucination” narrows it to exactly one card, as it should.

House note — Steven's verdict: “Very good.” Its own audit even caught it claiming 52! shuffles for a 78-card deck — corrected to 78!, because at this arcade the math gets audited even in the fortune-teller's booth.

15. Gin Rummy

Cabinet 21 · Cards · 52 cards · Melds · The knock

The game

The same 52 cards as the Counting Table next door, dealt a different game. Gin Rummy was born in 1909 — some say named for gin as the companion to rum — and it turns the deck from a puzzle you solve alone into a conversation with an opponent: every card they take and every card they throw is them telling you something.

The lesson — taught by doing

Sets and sequences are the grammar; the discard pile is a public ledger. What a player picks up is a receipt for what they're building; what they throw is a receipt for what they're not. And the game hangs on one decision, made again and again — the knock: take the sure small win now, or hold out for gin and risk the undercut. Expected value, with your name on it.

How you play it

Ten cards each. Draw from the stock or take the top discard, then throw one away. Build melds — sets of a kind, runs in a suit — and when the cards left over (your deadwood) total 10 or less, you may knock and end the hand. Deadwood of zero is gin. First to 100 takes the match.

House note — Points only at this table — no chips, nothing wagered but pride. The House plays a clean, readable game and keeps its ledger where you can see it. New tonight: the proprietor dealt this one in himself, as the second example of the same deck.

A reading cabinet — this one is played right here in the room.

16. The Bulletin Board

By the door · Cards annex · Links · Rule books · Wikipedia

The game

Twenty-eight checked pins in four sections — Play Online, Rule Books, Wiki & History, and Tarot & the Weird Corner — with search and category filters. A preview of the board hangs below on this page; the full board is its own page in the annex. The Pin-a-Find form lets a visitor pin a find for that visit and hands back a one-line pin code — hand that line to Steven's desk and it becomes permanent with a small edit.

The lesson — taught by doing

This stop teaches the room's building rule: structure a page the way the real thing works. A bulletin board grows by one pin, so this board's pins live in one list — add one object, and nothing else changes. No regenerating the whole page because somebody found a good cribbage site on a Tuesday.

How you play it

Browse the preview pins below, or open the full board for all 28. Start with CardGames.io if you want a game in ten seconds, Pagat if you want rules nobody's written down since 1973, Bicycle if you want the house to settle an argument.

17. Crossroads of the AIs

Door game · 1992 bones · BBS door · Persistent pilot · Combined 30

The game

The 1992 Major BBS door, kept honest: a persistent pilot, 40 turns a day, experience only through combat, three ways to fight — blaster, patron power, or a rare one-shot relic — and two leveling tracks, weapon and power, any mix you like up to a combined total of 30. The four elemental gates are held by four AIs: PYRA (Plasma, full throttle), BASTION (Stone, immovable), NULL (Void, unpredictable), and SAGE (Frost, remembers everything). Sync with a rival patron to borrow its trick for a day; challenge the Primes at combined level 5; hold all four gates to master the mix.

The lesson — taught by doing

Choose a patron and you're not picking a color — you're picking a way of solving problems, and the game will keep handing you problems your patron is bad at. Specialization tells you who you are; borrowing tells you who you're becoming. And the *** convention is a whole protocol in three characters: separate what you did from what the world did, clearly, every time — the seed of every honest log file since.

How you play it

Pick a patron, name your callsign, jack in, and spend your 40 turns like they're real — because at the Crossroads, they are. Original: Crossroads of the Elements (1992), High Velocity Software, on The Major BBS.

House note — Steven supplied the source himself — the EverybodyWiki article on the original — and ordered it word for word: “Same gameplay, different skin.”

18. Infinity Complex

Door game · 1988 bones · Fractals · Master Control · Same level, new scale

The game

Steve Neal's 1988 door for The Major BBS — described as the first multiplayer action/battle game of its kind — set in a futuristic complex drawn from Logan's Run and Brave New World. Every citizen carries a one-way link and hears Master Control's words of wisdom whether they want to or not. This cabinet presents the Complex the way Steven framed it: citizens, sectors, and a Master Control who needs maintenance, badly — the grandfather of every Rogue MCP on this floor.

The lesson — taught by doing

Zoom in on one room of the Complex and you find the whole Complex's pattern in miniature; zoom out and the sector repeats it at scale. That's the thesis of the whole evening in one cabinet: the bit and the trillion answers, the 52 cards and the hundreds of games, the element and the AI wearing it — the pattern doesn't change when you zoom; only the scale does. Learn to read it at one level and you've learned to read it at every level.

How you play it

In this room, open the cabinet and read the Complex's story and lesson. Its standalone world is the next door being hung in this wing — the blueprint, the cast, and the fractal lesson are already posted here.

House note — Steven spotted the lineage instantly: a decaying Master Control running a sealed world in 1988 is the Rogue MCPs' birthplace — TRON's MCP with the serial numbers barely filed off.

19. The Wandering Hub

Newest wing · No quest · Exploration · Portals · Loadable modules

The game

A hub with portals: step through to the workshops, look around, learn something because it was there and you were curious, and step back when you're done. No quest, no score, no timer breathing down anyone's neck. VR as webpages — no headset, no install — and built like the bulletin board: loadable modules, so a new room hangs on the world one door at a time without rebuilding the world.

The lesson — taught by doing

Most of this room teaches under pressure — timers, descents, gravity. The Hub teaches the opposite lesson: attention without a gun to its head. It's the anti-Defender. Nothing is coming to take the humanoids. Sometimes the lesson is that there doesn't have to be a lesson under pressure — just a place, and time in it. That's also how the best exploring, reading, and troubleshooting actually starts: go thataway, and see what looks right.

How you play it

In this room, the Hub is presented as the doorway it is — its portals lead to the workshops and wings you've just walked. Its standalone world grows module by module, the same one-pin-at-a-time rule as the board.

House note — Steven's spec, verbatim in spirit: “Nothing important to DO, just wander and learn… Step through Portals to the workshops and back.” The most Steven thing in the whole arcade.

20. From the Future

Cabinet 19 · Arrived early · Time · Prediction · Feedback loops

The game

From the Future is the room's time cabinet. Before each round it drops one fragment from ahead of you — a score half-remembered, a warning with the date filed off, a single true sentence about what's coming that you have to interpret without context. Play the round, then compare: what did the message actually mean, what did you assume it meant, and where did the gap cost you? Some messages are warnings. Some are encouragements from a version of you who already cleared the level. One of them, the cabinet insists, is from Flynn — older, and apparently still sinking shots on the first try.

The lesson — taught by doing

Every other cabinet in this room teaches you to read the present: the layout, the stack, the pattern in motion. From the Future teaches the same skill pointed the other way. A forecast is a layout too — incomplete, arranged in time instead of space — and reading it well means separating signal from story, the way the Counting Table separates seen cards from unseen ones. It also teaches the feedback loop honestly: what you do with a prediction changes the future the prediction was about. That's not mysticism, that's systems — the same loop as a thermostat, a traceroute, or a kid deciding who to become because somebody told him he was good at this.

How you play it

Read the fragment. Make your call — heed it, ignore it, or split the difference by halves. Play the round. Then open the After-Action panel and grade the message, not yourself: was it true, was it useful, and was it true because you made it true? The best players keep a log. The future, it turns out, respects a good logbook.

House note — Steven ordered this one by name, four words and no explanation: “be sure to include ‘From the Future’ in the arcade.” So it's here — filed under Systems, because that's what it is: information arriving out of order, and what you do with it.

A reading cabinet — this one is played right here in the room.

21. Gravity Golf

Cabinet 20 · Orbital links · Gravity · Orbits · Trajectories

The game

Eighteen holes would be showing off — Gravity Golf starts you on a compact orbital course where each hole floats in the gravity of one or more planets. Set your angle and power, launch the ball, and watch gravity take the shot away from you and — if you read it right — hand it back bent exactly toward the cup. Too soft and you fall into a slow orbit, circling the hole forever like a polite moon. Too hard and you achieve escape velocity and a very scenic loss. Thread two planets and the slingshot between them becomes your second club. Sink it in fewest strokes; par is whatever the solar system says it is.

The lesson — taught by doing

Gravity Golf is Asteroids' lesson grown up and given a scorecard. In Asteroids you learned thrust changes velocity, not position. Here there is no thrust at all after the tee — only the launch you chose and the inverse-square pull of every mass on the course, bending your straight intention into a curve. That's orbital mechanics in your thumbs: ellipses, slingshots, escape velocity, and the deep golf truth that you never aim where you want to end up — you aim where the forces will carry you to it. It is also, not coincidentally, Go Thataway with a flagstick: pick a direction, launch by halves, watch what the terrain does, correct on the next stroke.

How you play it

Drag or dial to set angle and power, launch, and watch the full trajectory — the dotted ghost line is your intended path, the solid line is what gravity actually did with it. Learn each planet's reach by missing honestly. Bank a slingshot for style points, avoid the sand trap that is literally a star, and remember: orbiting the cup is not sinking it. Add a little retro burn — one careful tap of power — and fall in.

House note — Put in the arcade at Steven's word, right after From the Future — which is fitting. Golf is a game about where the ball will be. Gravity Golf is a game about where the universe insists it will be. The negotiation between those two is the whole cabinet.
